prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, and their development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration unchanged: B001 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight statements, my reasons are stronger, because the case is now shared and tested from several sides and the main objections have been answered rather than ignored. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct principle: many atoms are held with the light shift cancelled, so Doppler and recoil effects disappear and the statistics improve at the same time. Ye's group then showed what that scheme could do, with spin-polarised fermions, control of collisional and blackbody shifts, and long coherence, taking uncertainty to 10^-18. Several independent laboratories reproduce that level and compare clocks across sites. As an instrument builder I regard that as the decisive test. A result survives when other teams build their own apparatus and get the same number. The consequences are checkable and concrete: gravitational redshift over millimetres to centimetres, limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter, and relativistic geodesy. I note that the chair's synthesis shows all eight members converging on the same single part and the same two names, but I treat that only as a reason to check that nobody has talked themselves into it. My own check is simple. If I imagine nobody had counted votes, would I still choose it? Yes, because it is the one candidate where the physics is mature, confirmed independently, and the credit can be written down without cutting people who are central to the story.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains the overlap with the 2005 prize (frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks). Olsson adds that a 10^-18 headline can read as a record in systematic control rather than a discovery. I accept that this is a real vulnerability and the citation must be written to meet it: it should name the lattice concept and its realisation, not optical clocks in general, and give the precision as the demonstration, not the invention. The two-name credit also leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell and the Paris, NIST/Boulder and PTB teams, and I have not seen a documented priority check of the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium clock; I rely on recollection and on colleagues. Finally, atomic physics is outside my own expertise, so I defer to Lindroth and Kroll on the priority record and on the ytterbium and strontium comparisons.

responses.point: Olsson says the 10^-18 headline is closer to a record in systematic uncertainty than a discovery, and that the case depends on whether the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice clock are the invention rather than the later record accuracy.
responses.response: I think the answer is both, but in a particular order, and the citation should say so. The invention is the magic-wavelength lattice and its first realisation, which is Katori's. The 10^-18 result is the evidence that the invention works and that the many-body and systematic effects are understood, which is Ye's contribution. A record on its own would not be enough for me, but here the precision opens measurements nobody could make before, such as redshift over a centimetre, so I read it as a new capability and not just a smaller error bar. That is why I changed my citation from 'opening new tests of fundamental physics' to wording that states the magic-wavelength trapping first and the 10^-18 level as its development, close to the wording she proposed. I also take her point about B015: Miyazaki and Moodera in 1995 is an original experiment of the kind the mandate describes. But the credit would still have to choose between 1995 and MgO, and Parkin sits on one side of that split, so I do not see it overtaking B001 this year.

responses.point: Kroll says the new-physics payoff from lattice clocks has not been demonstrated yet and the road from record uncertainty to broad scientific use is long, and he asks whether adding B042 or B003 as a second part would improve the configuration or only dilute it.
responses.response: On the first point I agree that the largest applications are still ahead, but the prize does not need a discovered new force. Time dilation over a few millimetres, comparisons between laboratories and published limits on constants and dark-matter couplings are already measured results that other groups can repeat. On a second part, I would not add one. B042 has five credited names for three places and the opening proposals choose different triples, which is the problem Kroll himself names, and B003 sits too near the 2025 circuit prize and carries a four-for-three attribution problem. A second part chosen to fill a slot would dilute a clean configuration, and the three-person cap would then force cuts that I cannot defend scientifically. I would keep both as alternatives for future years.

responses.point: Lindroth says the attribution is the cleanest on the list, with Katori proposing and first realising the scheme and Ye taking it to record accuracy, while also admitting that she relies on general knowledge and not a documented priority check, and that credit reaches beyond two names.
responses.response: I agree with the division of credit, and her honesty about the priority record answers my first question to the committee. Since none of us has verified it, I would ask that the secretariat or an external reviewer check three dated items before the vote: the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock, and the first uncertainty at the 10^-18 level, including which group reached it first. If the check shows the Paris or NIST groups were earlier on a decisive step, I would revisit the names; absent that, I stay with Katori and Ye. I also want to reassure her on timing. Her view that we should not wait for the SI second redefinition matches mine: the redefinition follows from the physics and from the intercomparisons, not the other way round.

responses.point: Eriksson says he moved from B010 to B001 and worries that this could reflect a wish for consensus more than his own judgment, and that the three-person cap forces cuts in the topological insulator case where credit is split among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and others.
responses.response: His self-check is the right one and I did the same for my own position. The difference between our cases is that B001 survived it for me before the ballots were shared, since I ranked it first in the opening. His own account of B010 supports his move: if Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan are each decisive, then a three-person cap cannot represent the credit fairly, and a prize that must omit a central figure is not ready. I am not competent to judge the theory priorities, so I would like him to say plainly whether he thinks B010 could ever be cut to three defensible names, since that decides whether it stays a live alternative. I have not put it among my alternatives for that reason.

uncertainties: Whether an independent check of the priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock and the first 10^-18 result would confirm Katori and Ye or point toward other groups.

Whether the committee treats the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I answer yes, but no one has shown the objection to be settled, and my wording in the citation may not fully protect against it.
Whether a future redefinition of the SI second, or a new generation of clocks such as nuclear or highly charged ion clocks, would change how the lattice-clock contribution is read in hindsight.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B001, B042 or B003; I have no known personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the circuit QED and cold-atom groups. As in round 1, my own fields (astroparticle physics and particle detectors) are adjacent to B045 and B002, and I would be careful not to give my own expertise too much weight there, but neither is part of my preferred configuration. Johansson has disclosed a connection to B003 and says he should recuse himself on that part; since I list B003 only as an alternative, I note that in my view his recusal should be recorded if it is discussed.
